Some patients have a single abscess.

The abscess presents with left upper quadrant pain.
Large solitary or multiple abscesses in a massively enlarged spleen can rupture into the peritoneal cavity.
The enlarged spleen is palpable or seen on imaging.
A massively enlarged spleen with abscesses is at risk of rupture; an enlarged spleen with impending rupture is an indication for splenectomy.

nodes.description: Standard antituberculous chemotherapy is the first-line treatment and can cure the disease without surgery: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, then isoniazid and rifampicin. Six months is recommended for isolated splenic tuberculosis and 12 months for widespread disease. Because the liver is often involved, liver enzymes and bilirubin should be monitored weekly. Glucocorticoids have been added for slow responders. Failures despite therapy are reported and led to splenectomy.

evidence.reference_title: Epidemiological Features, Etiopathogenesis, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Management Protocol of Splenic Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: The standard short course antitubercular therapy for 6 months is recommended for isolated splenic TB, and for widespread disease, 12-month therapy is recommended.

evidence.reference_title: Epidemiological Features, Etiopathogenesis, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Management Protocol of Splenic Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: Till 1990, splenectomy was the treatment of choice for splenic TB. However, with evidence supporting therapeutic chemotherapy, ATT has become the first-line treatment for splenic TB.

evidence.reference_title: Epidemiological Features, Etiopathogenesis, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Management Protocol of Splenic Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: ATT should be initiated cautiously, and weekly monitoring of liver enzymes and serum bilirubin is strongly recommended.

nodes.description: Caseous necrosis, and in the spleen frequent coagulative necrosis, destroys the centre of the lesions. The pathology series attributes the higher rate of coagulative necrosis than in the lung to the spleen's segmental arterial supply and lack of drainage. Large necrotic nodules give the central necrosis seen on CT.
